$$\begin{array}{ll} {\frac{1}{10}{\int_{0}^{10}{f(x)dx}}} & {= \left( \frac{1}{10} \right)\left( \frac{1}{3} \right)\left\lbrack {f\left( x_{0} \right) + 4f\left( x_{1} \right) + 2f\left( x_{2} \right) + 4f\left( x_{3} \right)} \right.} \\ & \left. { + \cdot \cdot \cdot + 4f\left( x_{9} \right) + f\left( x_{10} \right)} \right\rbrack \\ & {= \frac{1}{30}\left\lbrack {18.3 + 4(18.6) + 2(18.9) + 4(19.5) + 2(19.7) + 4(19.6)} \right.} \\ & { {+ \left. 2(19.8) + 4{(20.0) + 2(20.7) + 4(20.8) + 20.6} \right\rbrack}} \\ & {\approx 19.7} \end{array}$$

Fuel Consumption of Domestic Cars Thanks to smaller and more fuel-efficient models, American carmakers doubled their average fuel economy over a $$13$$ -year period, from 1974 to 1987. The following figure gives the average fuel consumption in miles per gallon (mpg) of domestic-built cars over the period under consideration ( $$t = 0$$ corresponds to the beginning of 1974). Use the Trapezoidal Rule to estimate the average fuel consumption of the domestic cars built during this period.
Hint: Approximate the integral $$\frac{1}{13}{\int_{0}^{13}{f(t)dt}}$$ .

image.alt: Details A curve is graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. problem.paragraph: In using the Trapezoidal Rule, the number of subintervals $$n$$ must be even.
In using Simpson’s Rule, the number of subintervals $$n$$ may be chosen to be odd or even.
Simpson’s Rule is more accurate than the Trapezoidal Rule.
If $$f$$ is a polynomial function of degree less than or equal to $$3$$ , then the approximation of $$\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx}$$ using Simpson’s Rule is exact.
Derive the formula

for calculating the cardiac output of a person in liters per minute. Here, $$c(t)$$ is the concentration of dye in the aorta (in milligrams per liter) at time $$t$$ (in seconds) for $$t$$ in $$\left\lbrack {0,T} \right\rbrack$$ , and $$D$$ is the amount of dye (in milligrams) injected into a vein leading to the heart.

Hint: Partition the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,T} \right\rbrack$$ into $$n$$ subintervals of equal length $$\Delta t$$ . The amount of dye that flows past the measuring point in the aorta during the time interval $$\left\lbrack {0,\Delta t} \right\rbrack$$ is approximately $${c\left( t_{i} \right)\left( {R\Delta t} \right)} \slash 60$$ (concentration times volume). Therefore, the total amount of dye measured at the aorta is
$$\frac{\left\lbrack {c\left( t_{1} \right)R\Delta t + c\left( t_{2} \right)R\Delta t + \cdots + c\left( t_{n} \right)R\Delta t} \right\rbrack}{60} = D$$
